sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Heard County, Georgia?
sections.html:
Heard County splits the work between two offices at the Administration Building in Franklin. The Tax Commissioner bills and collects, and the Board of Tax Assessors sets values and rules on exemptions and appeals. Knowing which door to knock on saves a wasted trip, especially if a sale is pending.

The county seat sits on the Alabama line in west central Georgia, and about 296 square miles of it are land. The Census Bureau counted 12,149 residents in its July 2025 estimate, spread at roughly 39 people per square mile in 2020. Many parcels here are rural acreage rather than subdivision lots, so tax questions often involve land value and returns as well as ordinary homesteads.

Heard County property tax offices, as printed on the county site

The Tax Commissioner page adds that the office has stayed open through the lunch hour since September 1, 2026. The assessors still close from noon to 1:00 PM. Call before driving over if you need both offices in one visit.

sections.h2: What is Heard County's history, and how does it shape its housing?
sections.html:
Heard County was created in 1830 from pieces of Carroll, Coweta and Troup counties, and it covered 301 square miles at the start, according to the county's own history page. Creek lands passed to the state after the Treaty of Indian Springs in 1825, and settlers drew parcels through state land lotteries. Franklin was an established village by 1770 and incorporated in 1831. Centralhatchee incorporated in 1903 and Ephesus in 1964.

Rocky soil kept farms small, and after cotton collapsed the county leaned on forestry. The county site says a large share of acreage is still held for the lumber industry, with some beef cattle and poultry and a number of factory jobs. That land use explains why so many Heard parcels are wooded tracts rather than subdivision lots, and why a seller with timber or acreage has more to discuss with the assessors than a seller with a city lot.

  • Courthouse: the building now in service dates to 1964, replacing one built in 1894.
  • Cities and towns: Franklin, Centralhatchee and Ephesus.
  • Border: the county sits on the Alabama line in west central Georgia.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers say about Heard County homes?
sections.html:
Heard County is small and affordable by Atlanta-area standards. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures show a median owner-occupied home value of $186,800 and 72.3% of housing occupied by its owners. Median gross rent was $917, and median household income was $65,868.

  • Housing units in July 2025: 4,979, with 4,309 households in 2020 to 2024.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 54.
  • Mean travel time to work: 34.9 minutes, a long drive to most jobs.
  • Households with broadband: 73.5%.

Only 54 permits in a year means few brand-new houses compete with resale listings. Older homes with deferred repairs are common, and that matters when an assessor's field visit or a buyer's inspection turns up unpermitted work.

sections.h2: How does Heard County assess property, and when are field visits made?
sections.html:
The Board of Tax Assessors determines taxability, value and equalization, notifies owners when a value changes, and approves exemptions. Georgia fixes the assessed amount at 40% of fair market value, set as of January 1. The county announced in a March 12, 2026 press release that it was updating its tax digest, with representatives visiting each property to photograph the front and rear of every structure and note changes since the last countywide update. The state requires that cycle every three years, per the county.

If an owner is away, a door hanger is left so the interior description can be checked. Ask the assessors at (706) 675-3786 whether your parcel was visited and whether new square footage, a finished basement or a replaced roof was recorded. Errors found early are easier to fix than after a notice is mailed.

  • Returns of value go to the county tax office between January 1 and April 1.
  • A taxpayer who paid last year and files nothing is treated as returning the same value as before.
  • Property record search runs through the county's assessor portal at qpublic.net.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Heard County assessment?
sections.html:
File a written appeal with the Board of Tax Assessors within 45 days of the date the assessment notice was mailed. The Georgia Department of Revenue says the appeal can challenge taxability, value, uniformity or a denied exemption, and it never goes to the state agency itself.

On the state's uniform appeal form you pick one route:

  • County Board of Equalization, for value, uniformity, taxability or exemption disputes. The assessors may revise the value and send a new notice, which you can appeal again within 30 days.
  • Hearing officer, only for non-homestead real property valued above $500,000.
  • Arbitration, for value only, which requires a certified appraisal within 45 days of the board's acknowledgment.

After a decision, a written notice of appeal to superior court is due within 30 days. Taxes must be paid at the prior year's level before the court hears the case. An appeal cannot argue that the tax bill is too high, because the millage rate is set separately by the governing bodies.

sections.h2: What changed for Heard County homestead filers and millage?
sections.html:
Heard's county site reports that House Bill 92, signed April 1, 2025, lets owners submit a homestead application during the 45-day appeal window that opens when assessment notices are mailed. Bring a valid ID showing your current address to the Assessor's Office. Statewide, the normal rule is to apply by April 1 of the first year you want the exemption, and failure to apply counts as a waiver.

The Board of Commissioners also published a notice in 2025 that its tentative millage would raise property tax collections by 18.29 percent. That meant 6.467 mills, one mill above the 5.467 rollback figure, with hearings held September 15 and September 23, 2025. Heard also keeps a posted history of tax levies for each year on the Tax Commissioner page, so you can compare rates before pricing a house.

sections.h2: When are Heard County property taxes due, and what happens if I sell?
sections.html:
Georgia's default due date is December 20, but the Department of Revenue says a county may move it to December 1 or November 15, or bill in installments. The Tax Commissioner page prints no due date, so read the date on your bill or ask the Tax Commissioner at (706) 675-3391. Interest is held off for 60 days from the postmark of the bill.

The person who owns the land on January 1 owes that year's tax. The Department of Revenue states there is no refund for partial-year owners, even when the house sells in early January. Ask the closing agent to show how the Heard County bill is divided and to confirm the payoff before the deed is signed.

If taxes go unpaid, the Tax Commissioner can record a lien and later sell the property at public auction. The commissioner posts a tax sale list each year, including a 2025 list revised October 17, 2025. After a sale, the owner or another interested party has twelve months to redeem by repaying the bid, added taxes and special assessments, plus a 20% premium, per Georgia's Consumer Ed office.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Heard County?
faqs.a: Pay at the Tax Commissioner's Office, 201 Park Avenue, Room 300 in Franklin, or mail to P.O. Box 519, Franklin, GA 30217. The phone is (706) 675-3391. The office is open Monday to Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:45 PM, including the lunch hour since September 1, 2026.

faqs.q: Who decides my home's value in Heard County?
faqs.a: The Board of Tax Assessors decides. Its office is Room 400 at 201 Park Avenue, phone (706) 675-3786. The Tax Commissioner only bills and collects, so value questions sent there will be redirected.

faqs.q: Is there still time to appeal a Heard County assessment?
faqs.a: Only within 45 days of the date your assessment notice was mailed. That clock is set by state law and printed on the notice, so check the mailing date on yours. Each new notice starts its own window.

faqs.q: Can I apply for a homestead exemption after the April 1 deadline?
faqs.a: Yes, in one situation. Since House Bill 92 took effect on April 1, 2025, a homestead application can be submitted during the 45-day appeal period after assessment notices are mailed. Visit the Assessor's Office with a valid ID showing your current address.

faqs.q: Does unpaid property tax stop me from selling my Heard County house?
faqs.a: It does not stop a sale, but the tax lien must be cleared at closing. Ask the closing agent for the payoff figure before the signing date. If the lien has already led to a tax sale, the redemption period is twelve months, and the redemption price carries a 20% premium.
